name: Maninka du Niokolo / Niokolo Maninka

catalog_quote: Il y a en maninka du Niokolo une forte dissymétrie entre ton haut et ton bas. En effet, on peut trouver des séquences de syllabes à ton bas de longueur quelconque, mais on n’a jamais deux syllabes successives à ton ponctuel haut. Plus précisément, les syllabes à ton ponctuel haut ne peuvent apparaître que si la syllabe suivante est à ton B, BH ou BHB, alors que les syllabes à ton ponctuel bas peuvent précéder n’importe quel type tonal de syllabe. Même si le système prosodique du maninka du Niokolo présente d’autres aspects qui poseraient problème pour une analyse accentuelle, il est clair que ceci évoque au moins jusqu’à un certain point le contraste entre syllabes accentuées et atones dans un système à accent de mot. new_statements.quote: Il y a en maninka du Niokolo une forte dissymétrie entre ton haut et ton bas. [...] on n’a jamais deux syllabes successives à ton ponctuel haut. [...] Même si le système prosodique du maninka du Niokolo présente d’autres aspects qui poseraient problème pour une analyse accentuelle, il est clair que ceci évoque au moins jusqu’à un certain point le contraste entre syllabes accentuées et atones dans un système à accent de mot. [p.25, 3.6.1:] Il y a en maninka du Niokolo deux classes tonales majeures de lexèmes : ceux dont le schème tonal ne comporte structurellement aucun élément haut, et ceux comportant un unique ton haut associé à leur premier PAT.
new_statements.translation: In Niokolo Maninka there is a strong asymmetry between high tone and low tone. [...] one never finds two successive syllables with level high tone. [...] Even though the prosodic system of Niokolo Maninka has other aspects that would be problematic for an accentual analysis, it is clear that this evokes, at least to some extent, the contrast between stressed and unstressed syllables in a word-accent system. [p. 25:] Niokolo Maninka has two major tonal classes of lexemes: those whose tonal pattern structurally contains no high element, and those containing a single high tone associated with their first tone-bearing unit.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The language is described as tonal (H vs L contrastive, e.g. ŋ̀ 'I' vs ŋ́ 'we'), analysed with H as the sole underlying/marked tone and L assigned by default. H is culminative-like in distribution: no two successive syllables bear level H, the vast majority of lexemes are either toneless (all-L) or have exactly one H on their first tone-bearing unit (initial syllable), plus a post-lexical 'demarcative' H inserted on a word-final light syllable before a following L-initial word. Creissels notes this distribution resembles a stressed/unstressed contrast but explicitly declines an accentual (word-stress) analysis; no stress accent is posited anywhere in the description.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned (no stress posited). The post-lexical 'ton haut démarcatif' (§3.7.5, p. 33-34) marks the final syllable of a prosodic word before an L-initial word; it is treated as tonal, not as secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Minor tonal classes with a non-initial lexical H (e.g. Bambáraŋ, kuŋkuwúlu, musénde; frozen verbal compounds like kálamúta), which lose the non-initial H in many contexts (§3.6.2, p. 25); words with a final floating H (baabaˊ 'papa', §3.7.7); proclitic pronouns ŋ́/í invariably H (fn. 2, p. 22); a supra-high realisation confined to ideophones/expressive use (§3.2.3).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the prosodic word including enclitics (§3.4.2, 3.7.6); 'compacité tonale' constructions treat noun+modifier / compounds as one tonal unit. Statement concerns lexical/post-lexical tone, not citation-form stress. Older Delafosse 1929 (pp. 104-105) claimed pan-Manding weak pitch 'accent tonique' on the word-final syllable and no tone; superseded.
new_statements.identity_note: Creissels 2013 describes Niokolo Maninka (mániŋkakáŋo of the Niokolo area NW of Kédougou, Senegal), which corresponds to the Glottolog dialect Nyoxolonkan [nyox1238] under Western Maninkakan [west2500]; Glottolog files the work under west2500. Creissels (§1.2, §3.1) stresses that its tone system is atypical for Manding (surface tones roughly 'inverted' relative to Mandinka/Bambara, one extra initial tonal inflection) and that Niokolo Maninka differs in some respects from the other Maninka varieties of Senegal Oriental and western Mali (the Kenieba Maninka dialect keni1246 is not covered). Delafosse 1929 is pan-Manding (Malinké/Bambara/Dioula) and not specific to this language.

new_statements.quote: 439. Il ne semble pas exister en mandingue de tons musicaux analogues à ceux que l'on rencontre dans nombre de langues négro-africaines [...]. 440. Par ailleurs, il existe en mandingue un accent tonique, un accent de durée et des accents d'intonation émotive ou logique. [...] 441. L'accent tonique, caractérisé en mandingue par la hauteur plus que par l'intensité, et très peu marqué en général, tombe comme en français sur la dernière syllabe du mot. 442. Si l'on a affaire à un mot composé ou dérivé, ou à un groupe de mots formant corps, il se répète sur la dernière syllabe de chacun des composants, mais se fait surtout sentir sur la dernière syllabe du dernier composant. 443. Cet accent est complètement indépendant de la durée des voyelles.
new_statements.translation: 439. There do not seem to exist in Manding musical tones like those found in many Negro-African languages [...]. 440. On the other hand, Manding has a tonic accent, a length accent, and accents of emotive or logical intonation. [...] 441. The tonic accent, characterized in Manding by pitch more than by intensity, and in general very weakly marked, falls, as in French, on the last syllable of the word. 442. In a compound or derived word, or a group of words forming a unit, it is repeated on the last syllable of each component, but is felt most on the last syllable of the last component. 443. This accent is completely independent of vowel length.
new_statements.citation: Delafosse, Maurice. 1929. La langue mandingue et ses dialectes, vol. I (full Gallica scan, ark bpt6k3412996f; 327 MB PDF not downloaded, scanned text saved instead).
new_statements.locator: Ch. I 'Les sons', 7° Accentuation, §§439-446, pp. 104-105 (scanned the text layer); accent de durée §§447-451, p. 105; notation note p. 28
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for west2500 has an empty rule; the existing statement (Creissels 2013, §3.4.1 p. 22) treats Niokolo Maninka as a tone language with a H/L asymmetry and a ban on successive H punctual tones (a tonal system with an accent-like statement). Delafosse 1929 explicitly denies tone (§439) and instead posits a fixed word-final pitch accent (§441), so it differs in type (no tone vs tone) and in placement (fixed final vs tonal H/L pattern). The statement is pan-Manding: the introduction (pp. 22-26) states that unmarked forms belong to the 'mandingue commun' and hold in all or most dialects; nothing in §§439-446 is marked for the western Malinke (MO) group, let alone Niokolo. It is…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Delafosse denies lexical tone for Manding and posits a weak, pitch-based 'accent tonique' on the final syllable of every word, 'as in French'; in compounds and derivatives it recurs on the final syllable of each component with the last component's final syllable strongest. He says its position is absolutely regular (§446, p. 105: 'son emplacement étant soumis à une régularité absolue'), so he does not mark it in texts or dictionary. A separate lexical 'accent de durée' (vowel length) is independent of it and is marked with a macron (§§447-451).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not called secondary stress, but §442 describes weaker accent on the final syllable of each non-final component of a compound (examples §444, p. 104: bolo-kã 'wrist', bolo-ni 'little hand', weak on lo, stronger on the last syllable).
new_statements.exceptions: None for the accent tonique (§446 calls its placement absolutely regular). For the length accent, §450 (p. 105) says the second syllable of a disyllabic root never bears length except in loanwords (wala < Arabic awlā, dyamā < Arabic djamā'a, kaso < French cachot).
new_statements.identity_note: Delafosse 1929 describes 'mandingue' as a whole (Malinke, Bambara, Dioula) and states (intro pp. 22-26) that unmarked forms belong to the 'mandingue commun' (kangbe) valid in all or most dialects; the accent section carries no dialect mark. The western Malinke group (MO: Gambia, Casamance, Rio Grande valleys) is the closest to Senegal-oriental Maninka, but Niokolo is never named. Creissels 2013 (existing statement) describes Niokolo Maninka specifically (= Glottolog dialect Nyoxolonkan nyox1238 of west2500).

readall_conflicts: Delafosse 1929 (pp. 104-105, §§439-446) says Manding has no musical tones and has a weak pitch-based accent on the last syllable of the word, repeated on each component of a compound; Creissels 2013 (existing statement, §3.4.1 p. 22) describes Niokolo Maninka as a tone language with a strong H/L asymmetry and a constraint against two successive H punctual tones. The two disagree on type (accentual/no tone vs tonal) and on placement (fixed final vs tonal pattern). Delafosse's account is a 1929 pan-Manding description written before tone was recognized in Manding, and is not dialect-specific; the modern, variety-specific Creissels sketch is the one to follow. The catalog reading stays as Creissels' tone language with a stress statement.
